titre: One Hundred and Three Years Without the Berne Convention
accroche: In 1886, ten countries abolish every formality for protecting a copyright abroad. The United States refuses to join until 1989.
contenu_vulgarise:
On September 9, 1886, in the city of Bern, delegates from ten countries, Belgium, France, Germany, Haiti, Italy, Liberia, Spain, Switzerland, Tunisia and the United Kingdom, sign the Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works. The text replaces a tangle of bilateral treaties with a single common rule: a work created in one member country receives, in all the others, the same protection that country grants its own authors. The convention enters into force on December 5, 1887.

The most radical point of the text fits in a handful of words, today in Article 5(2): the enjoyment and the exercise of these rights are not subject to any formality. A French author needs neither to register a play, nor to deposit a copy of it, nor to affix a notice to it, for it to be protected from the moment it is created, in Rome as in Paris.

## The country missing from the roll call

American law has worked the opposite way since the first Copyright Act of 1790: protection depends on specific formalities, registration with the Library of Congress, deposit of copies and, after 1909, a copyright notice affixed to every published copy. A book distributed without that notice could fall straight into the public domain, however original it was. Joining Berne would have meant dismantling that whole structure; instead, the United States chooses the more flexible Universal Copyright Convention, ratified by the Senate in 1954 and in force for them on September 16, 1955, and stays out of Berne.

The gap ends up costing dearly. As American cultural exports, film, music, software, grow in scale, works from the United States receive, in Berne member countries, a less automatic protection than those countries grant one another. On October 31, 1988, signing the Berne Convention Implementation Act, President Ronald Reagan describes the situation bluntly: American works protected by copyright, books, recordings, movies and software prominent among them, have been put at risk by the differences between U.S. law and the Berne Convention. The law makes the copyright notice optional for any work published after March 1, 1989, the date on which the United States finally joins the Convention, one hundred and three years after it was signed.

## A boundary worth remembering

This date explains an oddity that still puzzles research into the American public domain: a work published before March 1989 may have fallen into the public domain simply because a publisher forgot to print the copyright notice, an accident of form unrelated to the work's age or the author's wishes. A work published after that date keeps its protection, notice or no notice. The boundary has nothing to do with what a work tells, or when it was written, but with the precise day when two copyright systems, one founded on formality, the other on its negation, finally met.

carte.punch: Before 1989, a missing symbol on an American book could cost it its copyright.
carte.idee: In 1886, ten countries abolish every formality for protecting a work abroad. American law demanded the opposite, a deposit and a notice on every copy, which kept the United States out of the Berne Convention for one hundred and three years.

quiz.question: Why did the United States refuse to join the Berne Convention for more than a century?
choix: It found the term of protection set by the Convention too short compared to its own
The Convention excluded audiovisual works, then the main American cultural industry
Its law required registration and a copyright notice on every copy, which the Convention forbids imposing
The Convention granted copyright to the publisher rather than the author, the opposite of the American tradition
quiz.explication: American law required deposit, registration and a copyright notice on every copy, failing which a work fell into the public domain. The Convention forbids any formality as a condition of protection, which made the two systems incompatible until the 1988 reform.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many countries sign the Berne Convention on September 9, 1886?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Ten countries sign the text in Bern on September 9, 1886: Belgium, France, Germany, Haiti, Italy, Liberia, Spain, Switzerland, Tunisia and the United Kingdom.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which treaty did the United States join instead of the Berne Convention, before 1989?
choix: The Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Rather than Berne, the United States ratifies the Universal Copyright Convention in 1954, more flexible on formalities, in force for them on September 16, 1955.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What could cause an American work published before March 1989 to fall into the public domain?
choix: The author's death less than ten years after publication
Translation of the work into a foreign language
The absence of a copyright notice on the published copies
Resale of the work by a publisher based outside the United States
quiz_supplementaire.explication: American law required a copyright notice on every published copy; its absence, a simple publishing oversight, could make the work fall into the public domain, regardless of its quality or the author's wishes.
